messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 22
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Student
  trauma_type: Relief worker in war zone
  pcl5: 78

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Being Watched: Feeling watched or observed, Authority Presence: Police, Visual (Uniforms): Military or police uniforms
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event, Avoid Eye Contact: Making eye contact with other people, Avoid Uniform or Weapons: Military, police uniforms or weapons
  Negative Appraisals: Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kaito had always been drawn to helping others, which is why he volunteered as a relief worker in a war-torn country during his summer break. He was 20 years old at the time and had just finished his sophomore year of college. The experience was supposed to be a chance for him to make a difference, but it quickly turned into a nightmare. On one fateful day, while distributing aid in a crowded market, Kaito witnessed a shootout between rival factions. He saw people running, screaming, and bleeding all around him. In the chaos, he was separated from his team and found himself alone, hiding behind a stack of crates as bullets whizzed by. Kaito's memories of that day are etched in vivid detail – the smell of smoke, the sound of gunfire, and the feeling of being completely helpless. He remembers thinking that he was going to die, that no one would ever find him, and that his family would never know what happened to him. When the shooting finally stopped, Kaito emerged from his hiding spot, shaken but alive. However, the experience left an indelible mark on him. As Kaito returned to college, he began to notice strange feelings of being watched all the time. He would catch himself scanning crowded rooms, expecting to see someone in a military or police uniform lurking in the shadows. Even when he knew it was irrational, his body would react as if he were still in danger – his heart racing, his senses on high alert. Kaito started to avoid social gatherings and events where he might run into people from his past, fearing that they would ask him about his experience or worse, try to relive it with him. He also became increasingly withdrawn, avoiding eye contact with others and steering clear of any conversation that might lead to questions about the war zone. Kaito's friends and family noticed the change in him but couldn't understand why he was pushing them away. His grades began to slip as well, as he found it difficult to focus on his studies while constantly feeling like he was on edge. Kaito's perception of himself had also shifted dramatically. He felt like a failure for not being able to protect himself or others during the shootout. The weight of that responsibility crushed him, making him wonder if he was cut out for this kind of work. His body, once his trusted ally, now felt like an enemy – betraying him with its relentless hypervigilance. As time went on, Kaito became more and more isolated. He stopped attending classes, afraid of running into people in uniform or being triggered by certain sights or sounds. His apartment became a refuge, but also a prison. He was trapped in his own fears, unable to shake the feeling that bad things were always lurking around the corner. Kaito's sense of helplessness had become all-consuming. He felt like he couldn't stop bad things from happening to him or others, which only added to his feelings of guilt and inadequacy. It wasn't until he hit rock bottom – failing a semester and losing touch with his loved ones – that Kaito realized he needed help. With the encouragement of his family, Kaito finally sought therapy. As he sat in the therapist's office, fidgeting with his hands, he confessed that he was scared of losing himself completely. He was terrified that if he didn't get a handle on these feelings, they would consume him forever. For the first time in two years, Kaito felt a glimmer of hope – maybe, just maybe, he could learn to live with his past and find a way to reclaim his life.
